text: The OSI model is a conceptual framework, but the TCP/IP model is the one real networks, including the entire public internet, actually implement. It has four layers instead of seven, and it predates OSI as a formal standard — OSI was published later as an attempt to standardize something close to what TCP/IP had already proven worked.

TCP/IP's four layers, bottom to top: Network Access, which covers Ethernet and Wi-Fi — physical transmission and local addressing. Internet, which covers IP and ICMP — logical addressing and routing. Transport, covering TCP and UDP — end-to-end delivery between applications via ports. And Application, covering HTTP, DNS, SMTP, and FTP.

The two models don't split cleanly, but the standard mapping is: OSI's Application, Presentation, and Session collapse into TCP/IP's single Application layer. OSI's Transport maps directly to TCP/IP's Transport. OSI's Network maps to TCP/IP's Internet layer. And OSI's Data Link and Physical collapse into TCP/IP's Network Access layer.

You'll hear both vocabularies in real jobs, interchangeably — a firewall rule described as operating at Layer 4 means it filters on TCP or UDP port numbers either way. As data moves down the stack toward the wire, each layer wraps the layer above it in its own header, encapsulation: application data in a TCP segment, in an IP packet, in an Ethernet frame — exactly what a tool like Wireshark shows you as nested headers.
Next lesson: network topologies and physical media — the actual shapes a network can be wired in, and the cabling and wireless standards that carry the bits Layer 1 is responsible for.
